title: Lifecycles, Workflows & OIR
description: Explore how life cycle templates connect to workflow templates through Set State robot activities. Understand Object Initialization Rules and the gaps in out-of-the-box tooling.

topics.title: The Lifecycle-Workflow Connection

content.text: Life cycle templates and workflow templates are created in separate UIs, but they must be deliberately aligned. There is no automatic validation across the two — if the names don't match, you discover the problem at runtime, not at save time.
Two Separate UIs, One Shared Contract

Life cycle templates define states and transitions. Workflow templates define the process that executes a transition — who reviews, who approves, and the routing logic. The bridge between them is the Set State robot activity in the workflow, which references a lifecycle state by name.

State name mismatches cause runtime errors, not build-time errors. If you restructure a lifecycle without updating associated workflows, things break at execution time, not at save time. This makes mismatches hard to catch during configuration.
The Set State Robot Activity

The Set State activity is where the connection is made. When a workflow reaches a Set State robot, it tells Windchill to move the object to a specific lifecycle state. The state name in the robot activity must exactly match a state defined in the lifecycle template. There is no dropdown validation — it is a text reference.

cards.back: Defines which states exist and what transitions are allowed between them. The structure.
Defines who does what during a transition — the approval process, routing, and task assignments.
The bridge — a workflow step that tells Windchill to move the object to a named lifecycle state.
State names are text references with no cross-validation. Renaming a lifecycle state without updating workflows breaks at runtime.

keyTakeaways: Life cycle templates and workflow templates are created in separate UIs with no automatic validation.
The Set State robot activity bridges workflows to lifecycles by referencing state names.
State name mismatches cause runtime errors, not build-time errors.
Always update associated workflows when restructuring a lifecycle.

topics.title: Object Initialization Rules — What They Do

content.text: Object Initialization Rules (OIR) control what happens when a new object is created in Windchill — which lifecycle it gets, which workflow fires, which folder it lands in. OIR is the glue that connects type definitions to runtime behavior.
The Role of OIR

When you create a document, part, or change object, Windchill evaluates OIR rules to determine the object's initial configuration. This includes which lifecycle template to assign, which team template to use, the default folder location, and whether a workflow should start automatically.
The objType Value in XML

OIR rules use an XML configuration where the objType value drives validation at upload time. The UI type selection in the Create Object rule controls where and when the rule is applied in context. A verified hands-on test confirmed that when the objType value does not match the Find Object type selected in the UI, it does not cause an error when the document is created — the two values operate independently.

The independence of objType in XML and the UI type selection is not documented by PTC. No community post directly confirms or denies this. The hands-on test is currently the best available evidence — this is a documented gap in PTC documentation.

content.prompt: Match each OIR concept to its role:

pairs.right: Determines initial config when an object is created
Controls where and when the rule applies in context
One of the outcomes an OIR rule can configure

keyTakeaways: OIR rules control what happens when a new object is created — lifecycle, team, folder, workflow.
The objType value in XML and the UI type selection operate independently.
The independence of these two values is not documented by PTC — verified through hands-on testing.
OIR is the glue connecting type definitions to runtime behavior.

topics.title: OIR Gaps — Finding Rules by Type

content.text: Working with OIR at scale reveals a significant gap in Windchill's out-of-the-box tooling. Finding which OIR rule applies to a specific type is harder than it should be, and the workarounds require access that not all administrators have.
The Problem: No Filter-by-Type

The OIR table has a text search but no filter-by-type function. For soft types, the type identifier uses an internal branch ID format (e.g., wt.doc.WTDocument|8666) rather than a readable name, making visual scanning unreliable. You cannot look at the table and quickly find which rules apply to a specific document subtype.
The Workaround

A community-built QML report exists that maps branch IDs to readable type names. However, it requires report-building access that not all administrators have. No out-of-the-box solution exists for this use case.

This is a confirmed gap in Windchill functionality. If your team frequently works with OIR rules, consider building or obtaining the QML report that maps branch IDs to type names — it saves significant time.

rows: Branch ID format makes type names unreadable
Unreliable with many rules or soft types
Maps branch IDs to readable names
Manual maintenance, can drift from reality

content.prompt: Arrange these OIR lookup approaches from least effort to most comprehensive:
items: Text search in the OIR table — quick but limited by branch ID format
Visual scanning — manual and error-prone with many rules
QML report — comprehensive but requires report-building access
Manual tracking spreadsheet — independent but requires ongoing maintenance

keyTakeaways: The OIR table has no filter-by-type function — this is a confirmed gap in Windchill.
Soft type identifiers use internal branch ID format, making visual scanning unreliable.
A community-built QML report can map branch IDs to readable names but requires report access.
No OOTB solution exists for quickly finding which OIR rules apply to a specific type.

topics.title: Connecting the Pieces — Lifecycle, Workflow, and OIR

content.text: This topic ties together the three configuration surfaces covered in this module. When an object is created, OIR assigns its lifecycle. That lifecycle defines available states and transitions. Workflows execute the transitions. Getting all three aligned is the core administrative challenge.
The Configuration Chain

Object creation triggers an OIR evaluation, which assigns a lifecycle template. The lifecycle template defines which states exist and which transitions connect them. When a transition fires that involves a workflow, the workflow's Set State robot activity references a lifecycle state by name. If any link in this chain is misconfigured, the failure surfaces at runtime.

rows: Which lifecycle a new object receives
Wrong lifecycle assigned — object has unexpected states
Missing transitions — users cannot promote objects
Approval process and Set State activities
State name mismatch — runtime error on transition
Valid transition that no one can execute

content.text: When debugging a lifecycle issue, trace the chain from creation: What OIR rule fired? Which lifecycle was assigned? Which workflow is executing? What state names does the workflow reference? This chain-tracing approach identifies the broken link faster than checking each surface in isolation.

content.prompt: Arrange the configuration chain in execution order when a new object is created:
items: OIR rule evaluates and assigns a lifecycle template
Lifecycle template defines available states and transitions
Workflow executes and Set State activity references a lifecycle state by name

keyTakeaways: OIR, lifecycle templates, and workflow templates form a three-link configuration chain.
Failures in any link surface at runtime, not at configuration time.
Trace the chain from object creation to diagnose lifecycle issues efficiently.
All three configuration surfaces must be kept in sync when changes are made.
